A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GPT-4 translation study. Their full text, tables, figures, and Appendix A prompt templates are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-4 translation experiments on 1,017 sentences across three indigenous languages, including automatic scores, statistical tests, and qualitative examples.

after.justification: v2 retains these original translation experiments and their quantitative and qualitative results.

M1.justification: Both versions use GPT-4 with the same four zero-shot/five-shot protocols, with or without UMR, and chrF-based selection of five neighboring demonstrations. Appendix A preserves the actual user and system prompts.

E1.justification: Both evaluate translation into English using 506 Navajo, 406 Arápaho, and 105 Kukama sentences. The dataset description moves into Section 3.1; translation in the reverse direction is proposed only as future work.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparisons remain the same four GPT-4 prompting conditions. The expanded discussion of AMR and its applications introduces no evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: The sentence counts, translation direction, demonstration-selection procedure, prompting conditions, and BERTScore/chrF evaluation remain unchanged. v2's explicit statement that every item receives all four protocols clarifies the existing design.

E4.justification: The same prompting comparisons and two qualitative cases—Kukama forest-running and Arápaho storytelling—are retained with identical references and generated translations. Added source sentences document those cases; no new ablation, robustness test, or diagnostic outcome is reported.

E5.justification: v2 Table 1 first reports standard deviations alongside all 24 mean scores. The paired t-tests and their p-values are unchanged, and no additional runs or seeds are reported; both versions retain the limitation concerning repeated experimentation.

E6.justification: The only added numerical results are the standard deviations, such as Arápaho zero-shot chrF now reported as 13.0±5.5. All mean scores match v1 after rounding, all 18 p-values are unchanged, and the quoted translation outputs and performance rankings are retained.

T1.justification: Neither version presents theoretical results or proofs. v2's explanation of AMR/UMR nodes, edges, and rooted graphs is conceptual background, not a new formal definition or derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contribution: testing UMR and demonstrations for indigenous-language translation and finding statistically significant improvements in most comparisons. Rewording does not change the claims' scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning annotation cost, annotator training, and language fluency, and explains that reverse-direction translation would require speaker-based human evaluation. Section 4 also explicitly distinguishes the larger demonstration gains from UMR's additional benefit.

D1.justification: Section 4 newly supplies the source-language sentences for the two existing qualitative examples, making those cases easier to identify and inspect. The model designation, selection procedure, Appendix A prompts, and reported $62.11 experimental cost remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 expands the rationale for using UMR rather than AMR, adding multilingual-suitability and AMR-application references. It removes the brief annotation-work discussion citing Buchholz et al. (2024), Bonn et al. (2023), and Sun et al. (2023). This refines the existing research positioning.

P1.justification: v2 makes local wording and grammar corrections, expands the AMR/UMR explanation, and moves the dataset-description paragraph from related work into Section 3.1. The overall section structure and most methodological and results text remain intact.

P2.justification: v1's separate BERTScore and chrF tables become one full-width table with metric groups and mean±standard-deviation entries. The significance table is renumbered, and Appendix A places protocol headings on separate lines. Figure 1's graphic remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 modestly improves transparency through standard deviations and source sentences for the qualitative examples. Clearer AMR/UMR background, consolidated tables, and explicit annotation-cost and translation-direction limitations improve readability and scope assessment. The experiments remain unchanged, and the acknowledged need for repeated runs remains unresolved.
